prompt: How many hexadecimal digits does sha256sum print for the digest of a million zero bytes?
Match each property of a hash to what it rules out.

pairs.right: recovering a message from its fingerprint
swapping a given file for a different one that checks out
preparing two documents in advance, one to show and one to use

right_distractors: reading the file without the key

prompt: A log shows a file's SHA-256 as e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855. What does that tell you?
hint: The last line of the second capture.

choices.text: The file was a million zero bytes
choices.why: That digest starts d29751f2.

choices.text: The file was empty
choices.why: Right. It is the digest of no input at all.

choices.text: The hash failed and printed a placeholder
choices.why: sha256sum printed a real digest.

choices.text: The file was corrupted in transit, so it matches no list
choices.why: A digest alone says nothing about a list.

prompt: sha256sum -c printed agent-2.4.1.tar.gz: OK. Both files came from www.example.com. What has been shown?
hint: Where did the list come from?

choices.text: The file matches the list published beside it
choices.why: Right. Whoever controls the server controls both.

choices.text: The file is the one the vendor's developers built
choices.why: An attacker on the server could have replaced both.

choices.text: The file is signed
choices.why: No signature was involved.

choices.text: The server's certificate is valid
choices.why: sha256sum knows nothing about certificates.

prompt: A digest fetched from the same server as the file catches which of these? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A download cut short by a dropped connection
choices.why: Right. The truncated file hashes differently.

choices.text: A file damaged by a failing disk
choices.why: Right. Corruption changes the digest.

choices.text: An intruder who replaced the file and the list on that server
choices.why: The replaced list describes the replaced file, so the check says OK.

choices.text: A mirror operator who edited both files together
choices.why: Same case: both came from the one place.

prompt: You must detect a person tampering with a download, and have only a SHA-256 digest. Where must the digest come from?

choices.text: From the same server, over HTTPS
choices.why: HTTPS protects the transfer, not a server whose files were replaced.

choices.text: From a second download of the same list
choices.why: Same source, same answer.

choices.text: From a stronger hash such as SHA-512 on that server
choices.why: The algorithm is not the weakness; the source is.

choices.text: A place the tamperer cannot also change
choices.why: Right. Otherwise both are replaced together.

prompt: The shop's webhook accepts order=17&status=paid without checking any HMAC. Who can mark order 17 as paid?

choices.text: Only the payment provider, since the address is private
choices.why: The address is not a secret.

choices.text: Anybody who finds the webhook's address
choices.why: Right. The request needs no password.

choices.text: Nobody, because the body is hashed by TLS
choices.why: TLS protects the connection, not who sent it.

choices.text: Customers logged into the shop
choices.why: No login is involved in the webhook.

prompt: Why should the shop compare the received HMAC with hmac.compare_digest rather than ==?
hint: What does an early stop reveal?

choices.text: == ignores the case of hex digits
choices.why: It compares exactly.

choices.text: compare_digest also checks the timestamp
choices.why: It compares two values, nothing more.

choices.text: Timing would leak how many leading bytes matched
choices.why: Right. Constant time hides that.

choices.text: == is slower on long hex strings and lets requests time out
choices.why: The speed difference is the leak, not a timeout.

prompt: To stop yesterday's genuine request being resent, providers put a ___ inside what the HMAC covers and reject old ones.
A dispute: the provider says it never sent a webhook the shop received with a valid HMAC. What can the HMAC settle?

choices.text: That the provider sent it
choices.why: The shop could have computed the same code.

choices.text: Only that one of the two secret holders made it
choices.why: Right. Both sides can create valid codes.

choices.text: That the shop forged it
choices.why: The provider could equally have made it.

choices.text: When the request was sent, from the timestamp inside
choices.why: That does not say which side computed it.

prompt: How many bytes is the Ed25519 signature of agent-2.4.1.tar.gz?
After admin signed agent-2.4.1.tar.gz, who can read the file's contents?

choices.text: Only holders of release.key
choices.why: The private key signs; it does not lock the file.

choices.text: Only holders of release.pub
choices.why: The public key checks the signature.

choices.text: Anybody who downloads it
choices.why: Right. The file stayed readable.

choices.text: Nobody until the signature is verified
choices.why: Verification decides whether to trust it, not whether it can be read.

prompt: An attacker replaced agent-2.4.1.tar.gz, its .sig and release.pub on the download server. A user fetches all three there and verifies. What do they see?

choices.text: Signature Verified Successfully
choices.why: Right. A forged release checked against a forged key.

choices.text: Signature Verification Failure, since the key never left admin
choices.why: The attacker used a key of their own.

choices.text: An error, because a public key cannot be replaced
choices.why: It is a file like any other.

choices.text: Failure, because Ed25519 ties the key to the server
choices.why: Nothing in the key names a server.

prompt: ssh-keygen -lf on app and ssh-keyscan from admin both print SHA256:D69NpujcgW9pCTbA68lgiwW9k9fCvqO2C3xgQ55NwQk. What does that establish?
hint: One was read locally, one over the network.

choices.text: That the host key is strong enough
choices.why: Matching says nothing about strength.

choices.text: That app's password is correct
choices.why: No password was involved.

choices.text: That both machines share one host key
choices.why: Both lines describe app's key.

choices.text: The key arriving over the network is app's own
choices.why: Right. That is the comparison SSH asks for.

prompt: A backup script on a new machine stops with Host key verification failed. What is the fix the lesson gives?

choices.text: Disable StrictHostKeyChecking in the script
choices.why: That turns the check off.

choices.text: Distribute the servers' host keys to it in advance
choices.why: Right. The refusal was correct.

choices.text: Remove BatchMode so it waits for a yes
choices.why: Nobody is there to answer it.

choices.text: Regenerate the host key on the server
choices.why: The client still would not know it.

prompt: Order what apt does to trust a package, first to last.
items: download the list of package digests
check the list's signature against the distribution's keys
check the package against its digest in the list
trap: A digest is trusted only after the list carrying it is.

prompt: Match each system to what is signed there.

pairs.right: each connection, with the server's host key
the list of packages and their digests
the handshake, with each peer's static key

prompt: Why is plain SHA-256 the wrong way to store passwords?
hint: What does the thief of the stored values want?

choices.text: It has collisions
choices.why: That is MD5 and SHA-1.

choices.text: Its digest can be reversed to the password
choices.why: Preimage resistance rules that out.

choices.text: It is fast, so guesses are cheap
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is too long for a password column
choices.why: 64 hex digits fit easily.

prompt: Two accounts have the password summer2026. With a random salt per password, what is stored?

choices.text: The same value twice, since the password is the same
choices.why: That is what the salt prevents.

choices.text: Two different values
choices.why: Right. One guess cannot be compared against both at once.

choices.text: The password encrypted with the salt as its key
choices.why: Nothing reversible is stored.

choices.text: The salt alone, since it replaces the password
choices.why: The salt is stored beside a value computed from both.

prompt: A router's configuration backup uses an old, reversible password encoding. How should the backup be treated?

choices.text: As ordinary documentation
choices.why: It holds the passwords in reversible form.

choices.text: As safe, since the passwords are encoded
choices.why: Encoded reversibly is readable.

choices.text: As public once the device is replaced
choices.why: People reuse passwords.

choices.text: As a secret, and switch to the strongest format
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Thousands of customers must check that firmware really comes from the manufacturer, without being able to produce a valid check themselves. Which tool fits?
hint: Who may create, who may check?

choices.text: A SHA-256 digest on the download page
choices.why: Anybody can compute a digest.

choices.text: An HMAC with a secret shared with every customer
choices.why: Every customer could then forge one.

choices.text: A signature, with the public key given to customers
choices.why: Right. One key makes it, anybody checks.

choices.text: Argon2id over the firmware
choices.why: That slows guessing; it proves no origin.

prompt: Two services of the same company, and nobody else, exchange messages and share a secret configured on both. Which check fits?
hint: No third party needs to check.

choices.text: An HMAC over each message
choices.why: Right. Only the two parties need to verify.

choices.text: A SHA-256 digest sent with each message
choices.why: Whoever changes the message recomputes the digest.

choices.text: A bcrypt value of each message
choices.why: A slow password hash is for stored passwords.

choices.text: An MD5 digest, since the network is internal
choices.why: An unkeyed hash stops no person, internal or not.

prompt: One byte was appended to agent-2.4.1.tar.gz. Which checks in this lesson detected it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: sha256sum -c against SHA256SUMS
choices.why: Right: FAILED, exit 1.

choices.text: openssl pkeyutl -verify with release.pub
choices.why: Right: Signature Verification Failure.

choices.text: ssh-keygen -lf on the file
choices.why: That prints a host key's fingerprint.

choices.text: The HMAC of the webhook body
choices.why: That covered a different message.
